label: neurons 64 → 128, cold start
why: Run 3 is the matching 64-neuron cold start. With 128 neurons the 10-second stage was learned in 302 iterations against 804, and the best 10 s checkpoint scores 1.98 with F against 2.86 without. At 20 seconds the gap never opened in 400 iterations and the run was killed at 700. Faster to learn the short stage; no better at transferring to the long one, in the budget given.
mech: Measured for the speed-up, guess for the stall. More neurons means more wires, so there are more ways to build a working compass-and-tally from a random start, and gradient descent finds one sooner. The stall at 20 seconds looks like run 11's: the write gate settled high during the 10-second stage (fine for short trips) and at 20 seconds the tallies saturate; unlearning that habit takes many iterations regardless of size. If that guess is right, capacity is not what unlocks the transfer; the write-gate habit is.
llm: Model size. Scaling laws say bigger models reach a given loss in fewer steps, which is what the first stage showed. They do not say a bigger model escapes a bad habit faster once it has one; that is a curriculum and optimisation question, not a size question.

label: tally ceiling ±1 → ±2
why: Pinned cells at 25 s fell from 43% to 7.6%, so the lid worked as a lid. The count's error hardly changed (1.04 to 0.92 units at 25 s) and the score got worse, 1.62 to 1.96 (1.83 at the best checkpoint), with the first-3-seconds heading error rising from 55° to 66°. Saturation was not the leak.
mech: Measured. The decoding test shows the count's error growing in proportion to distance walked with or without pinned cells, so it comes from how the count is written and read, not from the ceiling: the write gate follows speed at +0.69 rather than 1.0, so each tick's addition is only roughly proportional to distance, and those small mis-weightings add up along the wander. The score loss on top of that is a warm-start cost: every readout had been tuned to cells that stop at 1, and 800 iterations at 3e-4 did not fully re-tune them to cells that reach 2, so the steering got worse. Guess: a cold start with lid 2 would avoid the steering cost but, given the count result, would not gain much either.
llm: Raising a clipping or normalisation bound. The general lesson is the same one this run taught: if the bound is not what limits accuracy, raising it changes the model's scale without improving it, and a model tuned to the old scale gets worse until it re-adapts.

label: train on 45-second wanders (stage 45)
why: 2.05 at 30 s against 1.62, and 2.51 at 45 s against the 2.15 run 19 scored there without ever training at that length. Memory still in F, compass cells unchanged at 32, but the reset weakened (erase at food 0.38 to 0.18) and the running score never came under 3.2.
mech: Measured for the numbers; guess for the cause. The loss is measured on the last ten seconds of a return that is now 90 seconds long, so the signal that reaches back to what the network did in the first 45 seconds is weaker and noisier than on 30-second trips. Each training step is therefore less useful, and 600 of them left the network worse than it started. The weaker reset fits: with less pressure from a clean board, the gate drifted toward fading.
llm: Extending the training sequence length (long-context training). The known caveat applies here too: jumping to a much longer length in one step, on a model tuned for the short one, usually needs a gentler ramp and more steps, and a loss that only looks at the end of the sequence gives weak gradients for the beginning.

label: batch 32 → 64
why: 1.62 at 30 s, identical to the parent; 1.76 at 20 s against 1.63. The running score on the training world was the best of any run (2.47), but the exam did not move.
mech: Measured. Averaging 64 flies instead of 32 halves the noise in each step, and the network fitted the two-speed training world more tightly as a result. That extra fit did not transfer to the steady-speed exam. Guess: the recipe has reached the point where the remaining exam error is not optimisation noise but a limit of what the network has learned to represent, so a cleaner gradient toward the same target changes nothing on the exam.
llm: Batch size. Larger batches give cleaner gradients and better training loss per step; when held-out performance does not follow, the model is at a capacity or data limit, not an optimisation limit, and the next lever is data or architecture.

label: erase penalty 20 → 5
why: 1.62 to 1.92 (best checkpoint 1.84). The gate barely changed: erase away from food 0.0077 to 0.0071, erase at food 0.38 to 0.31, write follows speed +0.69 to +0.75.
mech: Measured for the numbers; the cause is open. The prediction was that a cheaper penalty would let the gate fade between food visits; it did not (erase away did not rise). What changed is a slightly weaker wipe at food and a worse score, and 0.3 of score for that small a change would be surprising. The other explanation is that runs from the same warm start vary by a few tenths with the training dice. Run 27, run 19's own recipe reseeded, measures that noise, and this card's verdict should be reread against it.
llm: Lowering a regulariser coefficient. The general lesson holds either way: a coefficient found by a sweep is near its useful value, and before crediting a change to the coefficient you need the seed-to-seed noise of the setup, which is what the reseeded control is for.

label: a charge on the size of F (f_penalty 0.5)
why: 1.62 to 1.60 at 30 s, within noise. Write strength fell from 0.074 to 0.070 and erase at food rose from 0.38 to 0.51, so the board is kept smaller, but write-versus-speed did not improve (+0.69 to +0.62) and the exam did not move.
mech: Measured. The charge is on the mean square of F at the end of the episode, and the cheapest ways to lower that are a slightly smaller write strength and a harder wipe at food. Both happened. Neither changes how faithfully each tick's addition tracks distance, which the diagnosis says is where the count's error comes from, so the count stayed as accurate as before and so did the score.
llm: Weight decay on a memory state. The general lesson: a size penalty shrinks what it is applied to and the model compensates elsewhere; it improves accuracy only when large values were the cause of the error, and here they were not.

label: speed profile: two speeds → a new random speed every 5 s
why: Write-versus-speed rose from +0.69 to +0.77 as predicted; the exam gave 1.67 against 1.62, no change. The reset held.
mech: Measured. The many-speeds world forced the write gate to track speed more closely, and it did. The count's error did not fall with it, so speed weighting was not the binding part of the count's error either. What that leaves is how the direction is encoded: the compass cells are unevenly spread (six prefer north-north-east, six west-south-west, two bins empty), so the count's gain differs by heading, and the diagnosis tool now measures whether the error is in the count's length or its direction.
llm: Data augmentation aimed at one feature. The general lesson: augmenting the feature you believe is the bottleneck tests that belief; when the model learns the feature better and the task does not improve, the bottleneck was elsewhere.

label: stack: batch 64 + low-rate finish (3e-5)
kind: training (batch size and learning rate, stacked)
why: 1.62 to 1.64 at 30 s, within noise. Frozen checks during training reached 2.05, the campaign's best, and the exam did not move.
mech: Measured. Cleaner gradients and smaller final steps both improve how well the network fits its training world, and the frozen checks show that. The exam score is set by how accurately the network measures distance, which the diagnosis found to be about 0.9 units off at the turn, and neither change touches that. Optimisation is not the limit.
llm: Stacking two optimisation tweaks. The general lesson: when training loss improves and held-out performance does not, the model is at a representational or data limit, and further optimisation polish is wasted.

label: polish at a tenth of the rate (3e-5)
why: 1.62 to 1.71 (1.66 at the best checkpoint). The polish that gained a tenth on run 13 did not repeat here.
mech: Measured. Small steps settle a network deeper into the valley it is already in; run 19 was already at the bottom of its valley, so there was nothing to settle. The score moved within run-to-run noise.
llm: The final annealing phase. It helps when the model has not converged; on a converged model it changes nothing.

label: same recipe as run 19, training dice reseeded (seed 1)
why: Nothing changed but the seed of the training worlds, and the score went from 1.62 to 1.99. Memory in F, reset intact, compass cells 31. This is the size of the luck in a single run of this recipe.
mech: Measured. Each training run sees a different sequence of random worlds, and with a warm start at 3e-4 for 800 iterations the network ends in a somewhat different place each time. The exam then reads that place to two decimals, which makes small differences look like findings. The spread here, about 0.4, is larger than most of the gaps between runs on the leaderboard.
llm: Seed variance. Reporting a mean and a spread over several seeds is standard for exactly this reason, and a single-seed improvement smaller than the spread is not a result.

label: cold start on the many-speeds world
why: Learned the 10-second stage (exam 1.51 with F, 2.61 without) and stalled at 20 seconds for 900 iterations, like seed 1 and the 128-neuron run. Stopped to free the CPU for the seed replications.
mech: Measured for the stall; guess for the cause. Three of four cold starts this campaign and last have stalled at the 10-to-20-second transfer. The write gate settles high during the short stage and the tallies saturate on longer trips; unlearning that takes far more than the budget. Run 3's clean transfer looks like the fortunate case.
llm: Curriculum transfer failure. When a model tuned on short sequences does not extend to long ones, the usual fixes are a gentler length ramp or training on mixed lengths from the start, not more iterations at the new length.

label: erase bias shift −2 (slower fade)
why: The fade fell from 0.008 to 0.0012 per tick as intended, but the wipe at food fell to 0.06 and the readout never re-matched: frozen checks 6.06, 4.51, 6.37 at 100, 200, 300. Killed at 300.
mech: Measured. The exam-time fade test had already shown run 19's readout expects a count that fades with a time constant of about fourteen seconds. Lowering the fade hands the readout a count it has never seen, and the shift also drags the at-food wipe down because both live on the same gate. Training at 3e-4 for 300 iterations moved the network but not back to anything that homes. The fade and the readout are a matched pair; changing one by hand breaks the pair.
llm: Hand-editing a trained parameter that other parameters have co-adapted to. The general lesson: warm-start surgery works when the rest of the network can absorb it (run 7B); it fails when the edited quantity is one the rest of the network is calibrated against.

label: polish of run 29 at 3e-5 (many-speeds world)
why: 1.67 to 1.78 at 30 s, inside the noise.
mech: Measured. Same as run 26: small steps on a converged network change nothing the exam can see.
llm: Annealing a converged model.

label: same recipe as run 19, seed 2
why: Only the training seed changed: 1.62 to 1.61. With runs 27, 34, 35 and 36 the recipe has five draws: 1.62, 1.99, 1.61, 1.66, 1.73; mean 1.72, spread about 0.15, one bad draw.
mech: Measured. Different training dice, same starting weights and knobs, land in nearby but not identical places. Four of five draws are within 0.12 of each other; the fifth (run 27) is 0.35 off. That distribution is the ruler every other comparison tonight has to be read against, and none of the single-knob runs falls outside it.
llm: Seed replication. The mean over seeds is the number to report; the best seed is not.

label: same recipe as run 19, seed 3
why: Only the training seed changed: 1.62 to 1.66. With runs 27, 34, 35 and 36 the recipe has five draws: 1.62, 1.99, 1.61, 1.66, 1.73; mean 1.72, spread about 0.15, one bad draw.
mech: Measured. Different training dice, same starting weights and knobs, land in nearby but not identical places. Four of five draws are within 0.12 of each other; the fifth (run 27) is 0.35 off. That distribution is the ruler every other comparison tonight has to be read against, and none of the single-knob runs falls outside it.

label: same recipe as run 19, seed 4
why: Only the training seed changed: 1.62 to 1.73. With runs 27, 34, 35 and 36 the recipe has five draws: 1.62, 1.99, 1.61, 1.66, 1.73; mean 1.72, spread about 0.15, one bad draw.
mech: Measured. Different training dice, same starting weights and knobs, land in nearby but not identical places. Four of five draws are within 0.12 of each other; the fifth (run 27) is 0.35 off. That distribution is the ruler every other comparison tonight has to be read against, and none of the single-knob runs falls outside it.

label: cold start with a low erase floor (bias −7)
why: Earned the 10-second stage at 804, stalled at 20 seconds, stopped at 1500. Training raised the fade from 0.0009 to 0.014 per tick on its own.
mech: Measured. Started with a count that barely fades, the network learned to fade it faster than the warm-start lineage does. Third result in one night pointing the same way: the fading count is what training wants here, because a count that fades is easier to read with the tools the network has (a tanh readout of a bounded board) than a count that keeps growing.
llm: Initialisation choice from a cold start. It changes what is easy to learn first; it does not by itself fix a curriculum transfer problem.

label: erase bias shift −1 (slower fade, gentler)
why: Running score worsened from 200 to 300 (3.52 to 4.21); killed. Exam at 300: 3.07 with F, 5.91 without; erase at food 0.239.
mech: Measured. Same mechanism as run 33 at half the size: the shift lowers the wipe at food along with the fade, and the readout, calibrated to a fourteen-second fade, does not re-match in 300 iterations.
llm: Hand-editing a co-adapted parameter, smaller step, same outcome.

label: erase bias shift −0.5 (smallest step toward a slower fade)
why: 1.57 at 30 s, the reset intact (0.33 at food) and the fade lowered a little (0.0062 from 0.0077). Inside the recipe's noise on its own, but the first fade shift that did not hurt, which makes it a candidate for a ratchet.
mech: Measured. A half-unit shift moves the gate's resting point by less than the readout can absorb in 800 iterations, so the network re-matched; the −1 and −2 shifts moved it past that.
llm: A small initialisation edit that the network can absorb.

label: F-size penalty recipe, seed 1
why: 1.59 at 30 s. With run 28 (1.60) and run 41 (1.49) the penalty recipe has three draws: mean 1.56, spread 0.06, against the plain recipe's 1.72 over five seeds.
mech: Measured. The charge on F's size keeps the board smaller (write strength down, wipe at food up) and, over seeds, that lands about 0.15 lower than the plain recipe. All three draws are below four of the plain recipe's five.
llm: Seed replication of a regulariser

label: F-size penalty recipe, seed 2
why: 1.49 at 30 s with 38% arriving: the lowest exam score of both campaigns. Third draw of the penalty recipe (1.60, 1.59, 1.49).
mech: Measured. Same mechanism as run 40. One good draw of a recipe that is on average a little better; it is the recipe's mean, not this number, that should be quoted.
llm: Seed replication of a regulariser

label: stack: F penalty + shift −0.5, seed 2
why: Collapsed by 200 and did not recover; killed at 300 (exam 4.12 with F).
mech: Measured. Same shift, same start, different dice: two draws survived and one did not. The half-unit shift is at the edge of what run 41's readout can absorb.
llm: A fragile stack: an edit that works on some seeds and fails on others is not yet a recipe.

label: stack: F penalty + shift −0.5, seed 0
why: 1.66 at 30 s from run 41's 1.49. The half-unit shift lowered the fade to 0.0046 and the wipe at food to 0.21, and the score went up, not down.
mech: Measured. On run 41 the shift costs what it cost on run 19 and more: the readout re-matches only partly in 800 iterations, and the wipe at food weakens. The stack did not add; the penalty alone is the better recipe.
llm: A stack that did not add: test stacks at several seeds before believing them.

label: stack: F penalty + shift −0.5, seed 1
why: 1.64 at 30 s from run 41's 1.49. Same picture as run 42: fade 0.0044, wipe at food 0.21, score worse than the parent.
mech: Measured. Two surviving draws at 1.66 and 1.64 and one collapse (run 44): the stack averages worse than the penalty alone (1.56) and is fragile.
llm: A stack that did not add: test stacks at several seeds before believing them.

label: F-size penalty recipe, seed 3
why: 1.55 at 30 s and 1.40 at 20 s. Fourth draw of the penalty recipe: 1.60, 1.59, 1.49, 1.55; mean 1.56, spread 0.05, against the plain recipe's 1.72 over five draws.
mech: Measured. Four draws in a band of 0.11, all below four of the plain recipe's five. The charge on the size of F is the one change of the night that holds over seeds.
llm: Seed replication.
